title: Extraordinary Claims
objective: After this level you can explain why a surprising claim needs stronger evidence than an ordinary one.
summary: Hume: proportion belief to the evidence; the more unusual a reported fact, the weaker a witness's word. Sagan popularized the slogan. Hume's frost example: a higher bar, not a closed door.

cards.headline: Your friend saw a cat on the roof. Fine. She saw a tiger on the roof. Hmm.
cards.body: Same friend, same eyesight, same roof. Yet the first report is easy to accept, and the second makes you want photos, paw prints and a call to the zoo. That isn't unfair to your friend. It's good reasoning.

cards.headline: Belief in proportion
cards.body: The Scottish philosopher David Hume put it in 1748: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence." He added that the more unusual a reported fact is, the more a witness's word is weakened. It becomes a contest of two experiences: the testimony on one side, and everything you know about how things usually go on the other.

cards.headline: The slogan
cards.body: The astronomer Carl Sagan popularized the short version: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence." He wasn't first. The sociologist Marcello Truzzi had written "an extraordinary claim requires extraordinary proof", and the mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace made the same point long before. A tiger on your roof isn't impossible. It's just up against everything you know about your street.

cards.headline: A higher bar, not a closed door
cards.body: Hume's own example shows the rule isn't a way to dismiss things. An Indian prince who refused to believe the first reports of frost, he said, reasoned justly: water turning solid lay far outside his experience, so he needed very strong testimony. And ice is real. An extraordinary claim can be true. It just has to clear a higher bar.

cards.headline: Extraordinary claims: weighed
learned: Proportion your belief to the evidence
The more unusual the claim, the stronger the evidence needed
Sagan popularized the slogan; Hume had the idea
A higher bar isn't a verdict of "false"

questions.prompt: Who popularized the saying "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence"?

options.label: David Hume
options.rationale: Hume made the underlying point, not the famous slogan.

options.label: John Dewey
options.rationale: Dewey wrote about reflective thought, not this slogan.

questions.explanation: Carl Sagan popularized the slogan; Truzzi, Laplace and Hume had made similar points earlier.

questions.prompt: How does Hume explain why "I saw a tiger on the roof" needs more evidence than "I saw a cat"?

options.label: Witnesses lie more about big animals
options.rationale: Hume's point is about the fact reported, not lying.

options.label: The testimony must outweigh all your experience of how things usually go
Claims about animals can never be checked
options.rationale: They can; this one just needs more checking.

options.label: Unusual claims are always false
options.rationale: Hume's frost example shows they can be true.

questions.explanation: The more unusual the fact, the more the testimony is weakened: it's a contest between the report and everything you've experienced.

questions.prompt: Hume said a wise person proportions belief to the evidence. Which Level 1 idea is closest to that?

options.label: "Logic" comes from the Greek logos
options.rationale: That's the word's history, not a way of weighing beliefs.

options.label: An argument isn't a quarrel
options.rationale: True, but it's about what arguments are, not belief.

options.label: Only claims can be true or false
options.rationale: That's Level 3, and not about weighing belief.

options.label: Dewey: weigh a belief in the light of its grounds

questions.explanation: Both say how strongly you believe should depend on what supports the belief: Dewey's grounds, Hume's evidence.
